film.t: A chair knocked over. A meal left half-eaten on the table. And in the lighthouse logbook, a keeper's final words: God is over all.
That is how the story of the Flannan Isles lighthouse is usually told. Three men, gone overnight, from a rock at the edge of the Atlantic.
There's just one problem. The chair, the meal, and those famous last words don't appear in the official record.

film.title: THE LAST LOG|Case 01 · Eilean Mòr, 1900
film.t: So what did the men who searched that lighthouse actually find? Let's open the file.
About twenty miles west of the Isle of Lewis, in Scotland's Outer Hebrides, lies a small cluster of islands called the Flannans. Sailors sometimes called them the Seven Hunters.
The largest is Eilean Mòr. Sheer cliffs on every side, barely any flat ground, and almost no shelter from the open ocean.
Building a lighthouse there took years. Every stone, every tool and every sack of supplies had to be hauled up those cliffs from small boats. The light was finally lit in December 1899.

film.lab: James Ducat · Thomas Marshall · Donald MacArthur
film.t: A year later, in December 1900, three keepers were on the rock. James Ducat, the principal keeper. Thomas Marshall, his assistant. And Donald MacArthur, an occasional keeper, filling in for a regular man who was away.

Life there followed a strict routine. Clean the lens, trim the wicks, wind the machinery, record the weather. Every few weeks a relief boat brought supplies and rotated one man ashore, whenever the sea allowed it.
Keep one detail in mind. The island had two landing places, one on the east side and one on the west, because no single landing was safe in every wind. Remember the west landing. It matters later.
On the night of the fifteenth of December 1900, a steamer called the Archtor passed the Flannans on its way to Leith. Her crew noticed that the light was not shining.
For a lighthouse, darkness is the one thing that should never happen. A dead light is a danger to every ship on that coast.
But news in 1900 moved slowly. The Archtor reached port days later, and the report took time to reach the Northern Lighthouse Board.
The relief boat, the Hesperus, was due to make its scheduled trip. Bad weather kept it in harbour. It finally reached Eilean Mòr on the twenty-sixth of December.
Her captain, James Harvey, signalled to the island. Normally the keepers would come down to meet the boat. Nobody came. No one on the landing. No sign of life.
The relief keeper, Joseph Moore, was put ashore. He climbed the long stairway up to the station, alone.
The entrance gate was closed. The door was closed. Inside, the fire had gone out long before, and the rooms were empty.

And in the hallway, there was something odd. Only one set of outdoor clothing was left behind. Three men were missing. Two of them had gone out dressed for bad weather. The third had gone out without his coat.
Moore and the boat's crew searched the whole island. They found no one. Not a body. Not a single trace.
A temporary crew stayed behind to keep the light burning, and the Hesperus carried the news back to Lewis. A telegram went to the Board. A dreadful accident, it said, had happened at the Flannans.
Now, this is where the story you've probably heard starts to drift away from the record.

Popular versions describe a meal left on the table and a chair knocked over, as if someone leapt up in panic. Those images seem to trace back to a poem, Flannan Isle, by Wilfrid Wilson Gibson, published in 1912. It's a haunting poem. But it is a poem, not a report.
The official accounts we could find mention neither the meal nor the fallen chair.

Then there's the logbook. Versions online quote dramatic final entries. Winds stronger than any seen in twenty years. One keeper crying. Another praying. And finally: Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all.

But the official log's last entries are dated the thirteenth of December. Notes up to nine in the morning on the fifteenth were chalked onto a slate, waiting to be copied into the book. None of it matches those famous lines.
The dramatic entries surfaced decades later, in magazine retellings. The Northern Lighthouse Board has no record of them.
Think about what that means. The most quoted evidence in this case is a text that nobody can trace back to the lighthouse itself.
So strip away the poem and the invented log. What's left? An empty station. A routine that stopped. One coat on a hook. And the west landing.
On the twenty-ninth of December, Superintendent Robert Muirhead arrived to investigate. He had recruited these men himself. He knew them personally.

He went straight to the west landing, and there he found damage. Iron railings were bent out of shape. A crane was damaged. A box of ropes and equipment, kept in a crevice high up the cliff, had been torn away, and its contents scattered over the rocks.
This was not the work of ordinary waves. Whatever struck that landing reached far higher up the cliff than the sea normally does.

In his report, dated the eighth of January 1901, Muirhead set out what he believed had happened. The men had gone down to the west landing to secure equipment in stormy weather, and they were carried away by an unexpectedly large sea.

And the single coat fits that picture. Two men went down dressed for the weather. The third may have seen from above that something was going wrong, and run down to help without stopping for his coat.

Then one large wave, rolling high up the cliff, could have taken all three in a moment. No struggle. No panic in the station. Just three men doing their job, in a place where the sea can rise without warning.
Case closed? Not quite. Some questions remain. Why did all three men leave the station at the same time, when lighthouse practice expected someone to stay with the light?
Some researchers suggest a sudden rogue wave. Others suggest one man was swept in, and the other two were lost trying to save him. We will probably never know which. Their bodies were never found.

But here is what the record does tell us. The truth of the Flannan Isles is not a ghost, a sea monster, or a page of terrified last words. It's three ordinary men on an extraordinary rock, who went out to protect the light, and never came back.
The legend gave them a mystery. The record gives them something better: the dignity of what really happened.
The lighthouse on Eilean Mòr still shines today. It was automated in 1971. There are no keepers on the rock anymore.

s1.t: These are said to be the last words of three missing lighthouse keepers.
December 1900. Three keepers vanish from a lighthouse on a remote Scottish island.
The relief keeper finds the station empty. Only one coat left behind.
And that famous final log entry? It isn't in the official record. It surfaced decades later.
The real clue was down at the west landing. Bent railings. A broken crane.
The legend made it a ghost story. The record tells us what really happened.

s2.t: Three men vanished from this lighthouse. Only one coat was left behind.
Scotland, December 1900. A passing ship sees that the light is out.
When help finally arrives, the station is empty. No one is inside.
At the west landing, iron railings are bent and a crane is damaged.
Two men went down dressed for a storm. The third ran out without his coat.
One wave may have taken all three. The full file is on the channel.

s3.t: On a lighthouse, someone was expected to stay with the light.
But in December 1900, all three keepers of Eilean Mòr left the station at once.
The doors were closed. The fire was out. Nobody was left inside.
The investigator found storm damage high above the sea, at the west landing.
Did one man fall in, and two die trying to save him? Or did one huge wave take all three?
Their bodies were never found. What do you think happened?
